extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel and litigators advising on UPC proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide to the law, procedure and tactical considerations for litigating European patents (unitary and relevant conventional European patents) before the Unified Patent Court. Covers jurisdiction, opt-out and transitional rules, venue, procedure, remedies, fees, and substantive law (claim construction, added matter, sufficiency, novelty, inventive step).

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC competence (scope of actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has competence for infringement actions, declarations of non-infringement, revocation actions, and related counterclaims concerning patents that fall within its jurisdiction; this includes all forms of relief and protective and/or preventative measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC also has competence to deal with claims arising from decisions of the EPO relating to its function as granting/administrative body for UPs. The UPC does not have competence for contractual disputes relating to patent licences or ownership (those remain with national courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents within UPC jurisdiction (unitary vs conventional)
rubrics_metrics.description: European patents with unitary effect (UPs) fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the UPC; relevant conventional European patents validated in contracting member states also fall within the UPC's jurisdiction, subject to transitional-period rules and opt-out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the transitional period conventional European patents can be litigated in either the UPC or national courts; at the end of the transitional period any relevant conventional European patents not opted out will fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the UPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-arm jurisdiction / cross-territorial reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has 'long arm jurisdiction' to hear actions concerning European patents validated in non-UPC contracting member states and can award remedies (including damages and final injunctions) against defendants domiciled in an EU member state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples include decisions permitting UPC jurisdiction over UK and Swiss parts of European patents; the CJEU confirmed EU member state courts (including UPC) can make infringement decisions involving foreign patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out eligibility and scope (Article 83)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant conventional European patents can be opted out from the UPC’s jurisdiction during the transitional period; the opt-out only applies to relevant conventional European patents and has no effect on UPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An opt-out must be filed before any UPC litigation involving that patent; if an opt-out is filed before requesting unitary effect, a later request for unitary effect overrules the opt-out. Published applications can be opted out but will fall to UPC if they become UPs after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out timing, withdrawal and irrevocability
rubrics_metrics.description: The opt-out can be exercised until one month before the end of the transitional period; it lasts for the patent's entire life subject to a single possible withdrawal. Withdrawal of an opt-out can only be done once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An opt-out withdrawal will not be possible if the patent has been litigated before a national court during the transitional period; withdrawals are not affected by national proceedings brought before the start of the transitional period. If an opt-out is filed after litigation has already been brought in the UPC, it is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out proprietorship and declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The opt-out can only be exercised by the true proprietor or applicant; if there is more than one proprietor, all must agree and the filing must include a declaration confirming entitlement to opt out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False or inaccurate declarations render the opt-out invalid. Licensees cannot opt out. It is essential to verify proprietorship and obtain consents where necessary; the opt-out filing assumes the proprietor on registers is the entitled person, but the true proprietor has the right to opt out.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPC and patent joint opt-out requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where granted supplementary protection certificates (SPCs) in UPC states are attached to a patent, the SPC and the patent must be opted out together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not possible to opt out an SPC without the relevant patent, or vice versa. Where ownership differs between SPC and patent, all owners must agree to the opt-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional period length and possible extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 83 provides for a transitional period of seven years from the commencement of the UPC (expected to end on 01 June 2030), with a user consultation after five years that may extend the transitional period by up to a further seven years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opt-outs must be lodged no later than one month before the end of the transitional period (subject to any extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to start an infringement action (venue rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement actions should be brought before the Local or Regional Division in the contracting member state where the infringement occurred or where the defendant has residence/principal place of business/place of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action can be brought in the Central Division where the defendant is domiciled outside the contracting member states, or where the contracting state has no Local Division/participation in a Regional Division. An action against multiple defendants requires a 'commercial relationship' between the defendants and the case must relate to the same infringement (case law provides guidance on what constitutes a commercial relationship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Central Division competence for revocation and non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Central Division has primary competence for revocation actions and actions for a declaration of non-infringement; such actions should be brought before the relevant branch of the Central Division based on technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Central Division has branches (Milan, Paris, Munich) allocated by technical categories (A–H etc.), and SPC-related matters may be allocated to specific branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers and forum choice exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions may be transferred between divisions or heard outside principal rules where parties agree, where Local Divisions transfer part of a case to Central Division upon revocation counterclaims, where parties agree to transfer, or where panels handling related actions agree to hear them together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of filings can be decisive in determining where a case is heard (e.g., first-filed revocation vs infringement). Parties can justify selection of division based on residence/place of business of one defendant even in multi-defendant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcation of infringement and revocation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC is by default non-bifurcated, but bifurcation can occur when (1) a revocation counterclaim in a Local/Regional Division is referred to a Central Division while infringement is retained, or (2) a revocation action is already pending at Central Division and the patentee files a separate infringement action at Local/Regional Division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local/Regional Divisions have tended to rule on both infringement and validity together; bifurcation has been granted only in specific circumstances. In some cases a stay of infringement may be issued to prevent bifurcation, but stays are discretionary and decided case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of proceedings rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Local/Regional Division proceedings use either the official language(s) of the host state/region or an EPO official language (English, French, German) as designated; Central Division proceedings use the language of the patent; Court of Appeal uses the First Instance language (unless parties agree otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English is available before all divisions and is predominantly used. Parties can apply to change the language to the language of the patent; courts will consider all relevant circumstances, particularly the defendant's position, and fairness/convenience. Choosing a language must account for judges, parties and representatives who may be using a second/third language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation requirements and eligible representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must be represented before the UPC; lawyers authorised to practice before a court of a contracting member state and qualified European patent attorneys (with appropriate qualifications such as the European Patent Litigation Certificate) may represent parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-house attorneys may act as representatives in some cases but corporate representatives with extensive administrative/financial powers may not. UK-based European patent attorneys can act (no nationality/residence requirement). Best practice is mixed representation (European patent attorneys together with litigators) given the hybrid nature of UPC procedure and technical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge composition and tailoring submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: UPC panels include legal and technical judges (technical judges are typically senior European patent attorneys or former patent tribunal members); a judge-rapporteur (legal judge) manages the case and interim procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local/Regional Divisions generally sit in panels of three legal judges (plus a technical judge where invalidity is in issue); Central Division panels are two legal judges and one technical judge; Court of Appeal panels are five judges (three legal, two technical). Parties should tailor submissions to the nationalities/backgrounds of judges on the panel and consider prior decisions/orders of that division. Parties can agree to a single-judge hearing in First Instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-loaded written pleadings and CMS filing/service
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is commenced by filing a statement of claim or statement for revocation that must be quite detailed and contain all facts, evidence, argument and propositions of law relied upon; claims and documents must be filed electronically at the UPC Registry (CMS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC requires a 'front-loaded' approach. Service is effected by the date of access by defendants to the UPC CMS (case law confirms service by publication on the register can amount to good service). Defendants have three months to file a defence (and possible counterclaim); extensions may be available in some circumstances (e.g., international service or staggered service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written, interim and oral proceedings stages and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive First Instance proceedings comprise three stages: written (initial pleadings and replies), interim (directions, interim conference, clarification, evidence and experiments) and oral (hearing, examination of experts/witnesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim procedure should be completed within three months of end of written procedure; oral hearing is summoned about two months after interim and will be limited to roughly one day where possible; the written judgment should be provided within six weeks of the hearing. Aim is to conclude First Instance proceedings within about one year from commencement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim remedies: types and urgency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide range of interim remedies is available including preliminary injunctions, preservation/inspection/evidence orders (saisie-contrefaçon-like), asset freezing orders, and security for costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary measures are unlikely if the patentee does not act promptly — there is 'no fixed deadline' but the patentee's overall conduct determines urgency. Validity may be considered in preliminary measures but the defendant bears responsibility to challenge presumption of validity; courts have required defendants to focus on the best (e.g., three) validity arguments for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective letters practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Protective letters may be filed at any time to present evidence/arguments why a defendant believes they do not infringe or why the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a protective letter should be done carefully: courts may disregard vague letters that do not identify prior art or give detailed reasoning; an ineffective protective letter may not prevent an ex parte preliminary injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security for costs criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC may order security for costs where there is a risk that a party is unable to fulfil a costs order or the court may not be able to enforce the costs order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law shows security may be awarded where a party's means are inadequate; conversely security may be refused where the risk of non-payment is insignificant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final remedies and their characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Final remedies include damages or an account of profits (typically determined in separate proceedings), injunctions (discretionary and likely to be widely granted — no eBay-type rule in the UPC), destruction/delivery-up, recall from commerce, publication of judgment, orders for revocation, and costs recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim award of damages is possible pending full assessment. Costs recovery follows loser-pays principles subject to fairness and caps on recoverable representation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND defence handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants may raise a FRAND defence in SEP cases (arguing willingness to take a license on FRAND terms) which can potentially avoid injunctions and lead to FRAND rate determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPC has seen SEP cases; in reported UPC decisions FRAND defences have sometimes been dismissed and permanent injunctions awarded. FRAND issues may arise as counterclaims for determination of FRAND rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court fees structure (fixed and value-based fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court fees are a mixture of fixed and value-based fees: all actions/interim applications attract a fixed fee; certain substantive proceedings (e.g., infringement, declaration of non-infringement, applications to determine damages) attract value-based fees where the value exceeds €500,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed fees examples: ~€3,000 for a damages proceeding, €20,000 for a revocation proceeding; interim application fixed fees range from €350 (inspection/preservation) to €11,000 (interim injunction). Value-based fee bands run from €2,500 (over €500k up to €750k) to €325,000 (over €50m). Revocation actions and revocation counterclaims do not attract a value-based fee; revocation counterclaims attract the same fee as the infringement action up to a €20,000 cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee reductions for small entities and procedural economies
rubrics_metrics.description: There are fee reductions of around 40% for small and micro entities and further reimbursements where a single judge hears the case or the case is settled/withdrawn early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider entity status and single-judge option early to reduce fee exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs recovery rules and caps
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC follows a basic 'loser pays' principle under Article 69: reasonable and proportionate costs and other expenses of the successful party are borne by the unsuccessful party (unless fairness requires otherwise), up to limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC Rules set caps for recoverable representation costs based on value (from €38,000 up to €2m depending on case value). These caps may be raised in exceptional cases or lowered if they threaten a party's economic existence. Court fees should be recoverable in full; third-party costs (e.g., expert fees) are not capped and are recoverable to the extent necessarily and reasonably incurred. Unreasonable or unnecessary costs are borne by the incurring party regardless of outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship with EPO oppositions and stays
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition and appeal proceedings at the EPO remain available for conventional European patents and unitary patents and can run in parallel with UPC proceedings; opposition may be cheaper and remains an option throughout the patent's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPC proceedings are not automatically stayed because of EPO opposition/limitation proceedings except in exceptional circumstances (e.g., rapid expected decision). The UPC's approach has broadly been in line with EPO practice for many procedural/substantive matters but some divergences exist and are developing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and third-party access to pleadings/evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Orders and decisions of the UPC are publicly available, but written pleadings and evidence filed during proceedings are not automatically published; third parties must make a 'reasoned request' to the court for access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court consults the parties before deciding on access. The Court of Appeal has held that register and proceedings should be open unless the balance of interests favours confidentiality. A public requester must be represented by a professional. Courts have held there is no legal basis for awarding costs against a third-party requester in many instances, reducing the cost risk for access requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of claim interpretation at the UPC
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC Court of Appeal has held that the description and drawings must always be used as explanatory aids for claim interpretation, not only to resolve ambiguities — only after examination of the description and drawings does the scope of the claims become apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No statutory test for infringement by equivalence in the UPCA, but first-instance cases have applied tests based on national practices; Gillette/Formstein defenses and equivalents issues have arisen and UPC panels have considered national doctrines in their reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Added matter standard (gold standard and intermediate generalisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: UPC approach to added matter generally aligns with the EPO's 'gold standard' of direct and unambiguous disclosure in the description as a whole. For intermediate generalisations the UPC Court of Appeal has considered whether the missing feature is 'necessary for achieving the overall aim and effect of the invention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediate generalisations have been found unallowable where a feature was disclosed only in specific embodiments or where a non-optional feature is isolated from its original combination; the UPC's test may diverge in formulation from the EPO but often produces comparable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure standard
rubrics_metrics.description: UPC sufficiency approach appears similar to EPO practice: the patent must disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for it to be carried out by a person skilled in the art over the whole scope of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent fails this test the UPC may revoke the patent (case examples exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty assessment principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty in the UPC is assessed in line with EPO practice: decisive is whether the subject-matter of the claim with all its features is directly and unambiguously disclosed in the prior art citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second medical use claims are purpose-limited and patentable provided the specific use is novel and inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step assessment approaches and practical advice
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has taken mixed approaches to inventive step: the Court of Appeal has neither endorsed nor criticised the EPO problem-solution approach, leaving open the possibility of problem-solution, national approaches, or its own approach. Some divisions (e.g., Munich Central) have applied the problem-solution approach to enhance legal certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice is to prepare full inventive-step arguments both under the problem-solution approach and under national approaches (notably the German approach). Concepts to consider include 'realistic' starting points (multiple may exist), the skilled person as a 'team', motivation to proceed to the claimed solution without expecting particular difficulties, and the possibility of combining multiple prior art disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service, default decisions and good service standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Service via the UPC's CMS is effective as of the date the defendant accesses the CMS; the UPC may issue a decision by default for a defendant's failure to defend, and publication on the UPC website can amount to good service in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must ensure timely defence filings; where service difficulties arise (e.g., overseas defendants) the court may extend deadlines. Always verify procedural service requirements and act promptly to avoid default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-defendant suits: 'commercial relationship' requirement and joinder
rubrics_metrics.description: An action against multiple defendants can be brought only where the defendants have a 'commercial relationship' and the case relates to the same infringement; the concept can be satisfied by group membership and related commercial activities (e.g., same R&D, manufacturing, sale/distribution of same products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of a division may be justified by the residence/place of business of only one defendant if the commercial relationship test is met (case law example: SVF Holdco v ICPillar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out filing name accuracy and registry correction impact
rubrics_metrics.description: If an opt-out application is made in the wrong name it will be ineffective; corrections to registries can be made but an opt-out will be effective only from the correction date (not backdated), which can create problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the consequences of incorrect declarations, check proprietorship positions in advance and consider correcting registers before filing opt-outs where cost-appropriate. There is no official fee to opt out, but administrative and professional costs apply.
